newsitem.title: USA: Heavy feedlot placements to press CME cattle.
newsitem.headline: Heavy feedlot placements to press CME cattle.

text.p: Heavier-than-anticipated placements of cattle into large feedlots in key states during August and lighter-than-expected marketings are expected to pressure Chicago Mercantile Exchange live cattle futures Monday, analysts said.
"It got to the point where they (feedlots) made money and it was time to place cattle," said Jim Clarkson, analyst for A and A Inc.

The U.S. Agriculture Department Friday reported that cattle placements in feedlots with capacity of 1,000 head or more, were up 19 percent from a year ago -- at the high end of analysts' estimates of 106.6 to 119 percent and well above the average of estimates at 112.7 percent.
Live cattle futures were seen trading 0.025 to 1.000 cent per lb lower on Monday with the bulk of losses expected in December and February contracts.

"What the report has shown now in two months is the ability of the industry to rapidly make up for numbers on feed which I suspect will continue for another couple of months," said Chuck Levitt, senior livestock analyst for Alaron Trading Corp.
This put total on-feed cattle supplies at 92 percent of a year ago, up from 86 percent of a year ago the previous month.

"Barring any problems with the final maturity of the corn crop and the harvest period, by the time we get to the end of the year we are going to have very close to the same number of cattle on feed as the previous year," Levitt said.

Analysts noted that October futures will also be under pressure, mostly from long liquidation ahead of its spot position in about one week, and also from the less than expected August marketings. Marketings were a disappointment and should cause packers to continue easing their bids for fed cattle, they said.
August marketings came in at 91 percent of a year ago, near the low end of estimates. The trade had been expecting marketings to come in near the average estimate of 94.7 percent.

Even with one less marketing day in August "the 91 (percent) number just reflects that the cattle feeders were not quite as current on marketings coming into September as we gave them credit for," Levitt said.
"What this (low marketing number) will probably do is give the packers a little ammunition to resist having to pay over $72 for cattle," Levitt added.
Top prices for fed cattle in direct Plains feedlot trade the past two weeks were $72.00 per cwt.
